source.title: Primary School Curriculum Design — Creative Arts, Grade 5 (First Published 2017, Revised 2024)
source.notes: Read directly from 'grade 5 designs/GRADE-5-CREATIVE-ARTS-Curriculum-Designs.pdf' via the Read tool (no pages param), full text — all 3 strands, both optional sub-strands, the two Suggested Assessment Rubrics, Appendix I (CSL) and Appendix II (Learning Resources / Assessment Methods / Non-formal Activities). Official Grade 5 subject name is 'Creative Arts' alone (not 'Creative Arts & Sports', which applies only from Grade 7) — see namesByGrade on the subject entry in web/src/lib/curriculum.ts. Essence statement: Creative Arts at this level is an integrated learning area consisting of Art and Craft, Music, and Physical Health Education. Total suggested lessons: 180. Strand 2.0 has an optional sub-strand where the learner MUST cover ONE of Swimming OR Indigenous Kenyan Games — this build ships both as separate skills (g5-cas-swimming, g5-cas-indigenous-kenyan-games).

subStrands.name: 1.1 Wind Musical Instruments (Drawing)
subStrandBullets: Identifying: name, community, method of playing
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify indigenous wind musical instruments from Kenyan communities
Explain the role of the parts of a wind instrument in sound production
Make a wind instrument using locally available materials
Care for an indigenous Kenyan musical wind instrument
Draw a wind instrument using the crayon etching technique
Value indigenous wind musical instruments from Kenyan communities
keyInquiryQuestions: What is the importance of indigenous wind instruments in Kenyan communities?
Why is it necessary to care for and maintain a wind instrument?
learningExperiences: View real/pictures/videos of indigenous wind instruments from Kenyan communities and identify them
Name the parts of a wind instrument and discuss how they contribute to sound production
Source locally available materials and make a wind instrument while observing safety and clean the working area
Tune the wind instrument made for functionality
Brainstorm on the caring for a wind instrument and its importance
Take turns to practise care and maintenance of a wind instrument
Explore real/virtual drawings to discuss texture (cross-hatching)
Draw a composition of any two musical instruments using the crayon etching technique with emphasis on texture (cross-hatching)
Display and talk about own and others' created work using appropriate language
coreCompetencies: Creativity and Imagination — the learner searches for appropriate materials and ways of making a wind instrument
Communication and collaboration — the learner speaks clearly and effectively while discussing the care of a wind instrument and its importance
linkedLearningAreas: Social Studies — the learner applies the knowledge of indigenous communities to identify wind musical instruments from the Kenyan communities
scopeNotes: include: identification covers name, community of origin, and method of playing of indigenous Kenyan wind instruments
include: role/function of the parts of a wind instrument in sound production
include: care of a wind instrument specifically means handling, hygiene and storage
include: two named drawing techniques — texture via cross-hatching, and crayon etching (crayon sgraffito) applied to a composition of two instruments
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric 'Meets Expectations' rewards being able to create/execute wind instruments using locally available materials AND a drawing using crayon etching — both the craft and the drawing technique are tested.
subStrands.buildNotes: Instrument set (all real, documented Kenyan indigenous wind instruments, no invented names): nzumari and chivoti (coastal Swahili / Mijikenda), coro (Kalenjin animal-horn trumpet), oporo (Luo side-blown horn), nyanga panpipes (Kuria). 5 QuestionKinds (multiple-choice, categorize, click-match, ordering, fill-blank). No wind-instrument or drawing-swatch VisualSpec exists in the shared set — visual omitted deliberately for this pass, consistent with the other Grade 5/6 Creative Arts skills.

subStrands.name: 1.2 Football
subStrandBullets: Stopping (inside of the foot, step trap)
Papier mâché (shredding, soaking, pounding, mixing with adhesive)
specificLearningOutcomes: Execute the skills of kicking, stopping and dribbling in football
Prepare papier mâché for casting cones
Cast marking cones using papier mâché for a Football game
Appreciate playing Football game on a field marked using cones for enjoyment
keyInquiryQuestions: Why is the Football game popular?
What are the advantages of casting with papier mâché?
learningExperiences: Observe a virtual or live game to identify kicking, stopping and dribbling skills in Football
Demonstrate in-step kick and outside of the foot kicking in Football
Demonstrate inside of the foot and step trap stopping in Football
Demonstrate straight dribbling skill in Football
Practise kicking skills in Football
Practise stopping skills in Football
Practise dribbling skills in Football
Observe videos on casting method in sculpture to familiarise with procedure
Prepare papier mâché following correct procedure
Use a mould to cast papier mâché cones following correct procedure
Paint the cones for marking the playing area
Mark the playing area using the cones
Play mini football games within the marked field while applying skills learnt
coreCompetencies: Digital literacy — the learner operates digital devices to observe kicking, stopping and dribbling skills in Football
Creativity and imagination — the learner comes up with new ideas on how to improvise cones using papier mâché
linkedLearningAreas: Mathematics — the learner is exposed to ball trajectory as they practise kicking, stopping and dribbling
scopeNotes: include: kicking is specifically the instep kick and the outside-of-the-foot kick
include: stopping is specifically the inside-of-the-foot stop and the step trap (sole trap)
include: dribbling is specifically the straight dribble
include: papier mâché preparation is the four named steps — shredding, soaking, pounding, mixing with adhesive — followed by casting cones in a mould
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric rewards creating/executing marking cones using papier mâché, and the stopping, kicking and dribbling skills.
subStrands.buildNotes: 5 QuestionKinds (multiple-choice, categorize, click-match, ordering, fill-blank). No football-skill or papier-mâché VisualSpec exists — omitted deliberately.

subStrands.name: 1.3 Rhythm
subStrandBullets: Note values, symbols and their rests: minim, crotchet and a pair of quavers
French rhythm names taa-aa, taa and ta-te
Making a calligraphy pen (use bamboo/papyrus stick, fountain pen or any other)
specificLearningOutcomes: Interpret rhythmic patterns involving minim, crotchet, a pair of quavers and their rests
Create rhythms using music note symbols and their rests
Make a calligraphy pen for writing
Write in calligraphy French rhythm names of a rhythmic pattern
Aurally identify rhythm in two-beat patterns
Compose simple rhythms in two-beat patterns
Enjoy creating rhythms using music notes and their rests
keyInquiryQuestions: How can rhythmic patterns be created?
Why is calligraphy lettering used in writing?
learningExperiences: Listen to/sing simple songs involving minim, crotchet, pair of quavers and their rests and clap/tap their rhythmic patterns
Relate the French rhythm names to music note symbols and their rests
Practise writing the note symbols; a minim, crotchet, a pair of quavers and their rests on monotone
Apply composition techniques to create original rhythmic patterns and write them using French rhythm names and note symbols and their rests
Make a calligraphy pen using locally available materials while taking care of the environment
Practise writing letters of the alphabet (lower case) in calligraphy taking into account the angle of slants and ascenders/descenders
Write simple words in calligraphy among them French rhythm names
Clap/tap/stamp the beat/pulse and identify the strong and weak beats of music in two-beat patterns
Sing or listen to different types of songs and rhythmic patterns to identify two-beat patterns
Compose two-beat rhythmic patterns
Present composed rhythmic patterns to peers for review and feedback
coreCompetencies: Communication and collaboration — the learner listens keenly to peers' presentations on rhythmic patterns and speaks clearly to provide feedback
Creativity and Imagination — the learner utilises the composition techniques to compose original rhythmic patterns in two-beat patterns
Learning to Learn — the learner takes initiative to understand how rhythmic patterns are created
linkedLearningAreas: English — the learner uses the knowledge of the alphabet to practise writing in calligraphy
scopeNotes: include: note values are exactly minim (2 beats), crotchet (1 beat), a pair of quavers (1 beat total), plus their rests
include: French rhythm names are exactly taa-aa (minim), taa (crotchet), ta-te (pair of quavers)
include: calligraphy covers making a pen from a bamboo/papyrus stick and writing with a consistent slant, ascenders and descenders
include: metre work is limited to two-beat patterns — identifying strong (beat 1) and weak (beat 2) beats, and composing two-beat rhythms
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric rewards creating rhythms using note values and rests, and making a calligraphy pen for writing.
subStrands.buildNotes: 6 QuestionKinds (multiple-choice, click-match, categorize, number-line, ordering, fill-blank). Uses the registered { type: 'music-note' } VisualSpec for note/rest recognition (crotchet, quaver-pair, minim, crotchet-rest, minim-rest). number-line branch totals the beats of an rng-built pattern of French rhythm names.

subStrands.name: 1.4 Painting and Mosaic
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify primary and secondary colours on the colour wheel
Paint a scenery composition using the wash technique
Prepare materials for making a mosaic picture
Create a mosaic picture to apply the characteristics
Appreciate painting and mosaic as picture making techniques
keyInquiryQuestions: How do we use pictures in our daily lives?
learningExperiences: Paint a colour wheel with primary and secondary colours
Demonstrate wash out technique of painting (flat and graded wash)
Paint a simple composition of a scenery using washout technique with focus on colour value
Observe real/virtual mosaic pictures to identify materials and characteristics
Collect and prepare materials for making mosaic; recyclable coloured paper or banana fibres, suitable adhesives and supports
Paint the support in one colour to contrast the pasted material
Sketch on the support one form; a fruit/bird/animal or any other
Create a mosaic with emphasis on: mono media and spacing of the materials
Display and talk about own and others work in a just manner
coreCompetencies: Creativity and Imagination — the learner generates original ideas and expresses them through a painting or mosaic picture
Critical Thinking and Problem solving — the learner analyses and evaluates choices in colour and technique to make pictures
linkedLearningAreas: Science and Technology — the learner understands the concepts of colour classification into primary and secondary colours
Mathematics — the learner explores geometric patterns in mosaic compositions
scopeNotes: include: colour wheel work is primary (red, yellow, blue) and secondary (orange, green, purple) colours only
include: wash technique is specifically the flat wash and the graded wash, with focus on colour value (lightness/darkness)
include: mosaic materials are recyclable coloured paper OR banana fibres, plus suitable adhesives and a support
include: making the mosaic emphasises mono media (one type of material) and even spacing between the pieces; the support is painted one contrasting colour first
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric rewards painting a scenery composition (wash technique). Core Competencies box names 'Critical Thinking and Problem solving' — so the skill carries at least one Evaluate-tier branch (judging colour/technique choices against a stated goal), per RIGOR-STANDARDS.md.
subStrands.buildNotes: 5 QuestionKinds (multiple-choice, categorize, click-match, ordering, fill-blank). Uses the registered { type: 'color-wheel' } VisualSpec (highlight primary/secondary).

subStrands.name: 1.5 Melody
subStrandBullets: Sol-fa syllables: d r m f s
Kodaly hand signs: d r m f s
Composition techniques: Stepwise motion, narrow leaps, repetition of pitches, variation of pitches, ending on a long note
Qualities of a card: (layout, colour, lettering)
specificLearningOutcomes: Sing the sol-fa syllables d r m f s for pitch discrimination
Interpret the hand signs of the sol-fa syllables d r m f s
Compose short melodies based on the sol-fa syllables d r m f s
Make a decorated melody card for creativity
Appreciate melodies created by self and others
keyInquiryQuestions: Why is it necessary to apply composition techniques in composing a melody?
learningExperiences: Sing familiar songs based on the sol-fa syllables d r m f s
Sing the sol-fa syllables in ascending and descending order
Search for videos or watch live demonstrations of the Kodaly hand signs for d r m f s and practise performing the hand signs
Orally and aurally identify the pitches d r m f s displayed on cards or played on a melodic instrument
Collaboratively play melody games such as question and answer phrases, completing a given phrase orally
Listen to songs and discuss the composition techniques used
Apply compositional techniques to create short melodies using the sol-fa syllables d r m f s and the note values learnt observing integrity
Measure, cut and fold paper to create card layout (use a hard coloured paper)
Write own created melody (using either French rhythm names or note symbols) on the card neatly
Cut out and paste assorted coloured papers to decorate the card while observing safety
coreCompetencies: Self-efficacy — the learner creates original melodies and records them using digital devices
Digital literacy — the learner uses digital devices to search and watch videos of hand signs
Creativity and imagination — the learner explores the sol-fa syllables and note values to create original melodies and cards
linkedLearningAreas: English — the learner articulates vowels and syllables as they sing the sol-fa scale reinforcing language skills
scopeNotes: include: sol-fa is limited to the five syllables d r m f s (doh, re, me, fah, soh)
include: Kodaly hand signs for those same five syllables
include: the five named composition techniques — stepwise motion, narrow leaps, repetition of pitches, variation of pitches, ending on a long note
include: card qualities are exactly layout, colour and lettering; the card carries the learner's own written melody
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric rewards creating short melodies using d r m f s and performing the hand signs of the sol-fa syllables d r m f s.
subStrands.buildNotes: 6 QuestionKinds (multiple-choice, ordering, click-match, categorize, number-line, fill-blank). Uses the registered { type: 'sol-fa-ladder' } VisualSpec (highlight doh/re/me/fah/soh). number-line branch marks a syllable's scale-degree position (doh=1 .. soh=5).

subStrands.name: 1.6 Rounders
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify the features of a rounders bat for familiarisation
Identify materials and tools used in carving
Carve a bat for playing the Rounders game
Execute batting and fielding skills in a Rounders game for skills acquisition
Value the safety of self and others when playing the game of Rounders
keyInquiryQuestions: How do fielding skills help players in a Rounders game?
learningExperiences: Observe illustrations or actual samples of rounders bats to identify the features (knob, handle, grip, head, length and thickness)
Watch videos/pictures on the carving technique for familiarisation
Assemble materials and tools for carving a bat with a focus on wood-cutting tools
Collaboratively, use locally available wood to carve rounders' bats while observing safety
Demonstrate batting skills
Practise batting using the improvised bat
Practise fielding skills
Play a Rounders game while observing safety
coreCompetencies: Communication and Collaboration — the learner talks, shares materials and ideas on executing the skill of batting, fielding when playing Rounders
Creativity and Imagination — the learner works with peers and exchange new ideas to inspire creativity when carving the bat
linkedLearningAreas: Mathematics — the learner acquires concepts of order and counting while practising fielding and batting
scopeNotes: include: bat features are exactly knob, handle, grip, head, length and thickness
include: carving focuses on wood-cutting tools (saw, chisel, gouge, whittling knife, rasp) and locally available wood, with safety of self and others
include: skills are batting and fielding; fielding's role (catching to dismiss, limiting runs) is the key inquiry
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric rewards creating/executing a bat for playing Rounders and the batting and fielding skills.
subStrands.buildNotes: 5 QuestionKinds (multiple-choice, categorize, click-match, ordering, fill-blank). No rounders-bat or carving-tool VisualSpec exists — omitted deliberately.

subStrands.name: 2.1 Athletics
specificLearningOutcomes: Improvise batons for relay racing
Make ropes using plaiting technique for relay racing
Perform the skill of visual baton change in a relay race
Execute nonvisual baton change in a relay race
Appraise self and peers' performance in a relay race
keyInquiryQuestions: Why is observance of the visual and non-visual baton change skill important in a relay race?
How are plaiting materials prepared?
learningExperiences: Collect appropriate locally available materials for making batons (plastic, wood, bamboo, aluminium) and improvise a baton
Explore actual and virtual samples of plaited basketry items
Collect materials for plaiting a rope (sisal, leather, old fabric)
Prepare and decorate the material for ropes by cutting to size and dyeing/painting
Plait a 3-strand rope for use as tape for ending races
Demonstrate the skill of baton change (upsweep)
Demonstrate the skills of baton change (down sweep)
Practise the skill of baton change in a relay race while observing safety
Participate in a relay race with peers running towards the finishing tape
coreCompetencies: Creativity and Imagination — the learner comes up with new ideas on how to improvise a baton
Learning to learn — the learner acquires new skills of baton change (upsweep and down sweep)
linkedLearningAreas: Mathematics — the learner uses concepts of measuring to make an improvised baton for relay
scopeNotes: include: baton change is exactly the upsweep and the downsweep
include: relay skills also distinguish the visual baton change (receiver looks back) from the non-visual baton change (receiver eyes-forward, on a call)
include: baton materials are plastic, wood, bamboo, aluminium
include: plaiting is a 3-strand rope from sisal, leather or old fabric, prepared by cutting to size and dyeing/painting, used as the finishing tape
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric rewards performing/displaying batons for relay racing and baton change in a relay race.
subStrands.buildNotes: 5 QuestionKinds (multiple-choice, categorize, click-match, ordering, fill-blank). No relay-changeover or plaiting VisualSpec exists — omitted deliberately.

subStrands.name: 2.2 Fabric Decoration
subStrandBullets: Materials (dyes, tying materials, cotton fabric, dye fasteners)
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify techniques used to decorate a fabric
Decorate a fabric using the tie and dye technique
Decorate a fabric using appliqué for expression
Value tie and dye and appliqué techniques for decorating a fabric
keyInquiryQuestions: Why is fabric decoration important?
What are the sources of natural dyes?
learningExperiences: Explore virtual and actual sources to identify fabrics decorated using tie and dye (circle) and appliqué
Source materials such as recyclable fabrics, tying/stitching/pasting materials and dye (natural/artificial)
Prepare the dye bathe (primary colour) using dyes, water and fasteners
Explore tying the fabrics in varied ways using circle techniques
Dye in one colour, untie and iron
Decorate the fabric using appliqué technique with emphasis on; contrast of the surface and pasted fabrics (colour/patterns) using stitching or pasting method
Neaten the decorated fabrics by trimming and ironing
Show and talk about own and others decorated fabrics
coreCompetencies: Digital literacy — the learner explores virtual and actual sources to study techniques of fabric decoration
Creativity and imagination — the learner decorates the fabric using appliqué technique
linkedLearningAreas: Agriculture — the learner studies techniques of fabric decoration focusing on tie and dye, appliqué and materials in fabric decoration
scopeNotes: include: named materials are dyes, tying materials, cotton fabric, dye fasteners (fixatives/salt)
include: tie and dye is specifically the circle technique, dyed in one primary colour, then untied and ironed
include: appliqué emphasises contrast (colour/pattern) between the surface and pasted fabrics, attached by stitching OR pasting, then neatened by trimming and ironing
include: sources of natural dyes are an explicit key inquiry question
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric rewards performing/displaying decorated fabric using tie and dye AND decorated fabric using appliqué — both techniques are tested.
subStrands.buildNotes: 5 QuestionKinds (multiple-choice, categorize, click-match, ordering, fill-blank). The ordering branch randomly runs the tie-and-dye OR the appliqué process. No tie-dye/appliqué VisualSpec exists — omitted deliberately.

subStrands.name: 2.3 Kenyan Folk Dance
subStrandBullets: Background of the dance: name, community of origin, performers (soloist, chorus/response, instrumentalist, dancers), occasion
Components of a dance: songs, costumes, body movements, adornment, ornaments, formations, props and instruments
Performance components: songs, body movements, formations and patterns, instruments, costumes, body adornment, ornaments, props, safety and etiquette
specificLearningOutcomes: Discuss the background of a Kenyan folk dance
Describe components of a Kenyan folk dance
Discuss the roles of folk dance in the community
Make an ornament using available materials to enhance performance of a Kenyan folk dance
Perform in a folk dance from a Kenyan indigenous community
Acknowledge the role of folk dance in the society
keyInquiryQuestions: Why is it necessary to perform a folk dance?
How do the components of a folk dance contribute to its performance?
learningExperiences: Watch a Kenyan folk-dance performance and discuss the background details
Identify and describe the components of a Kenyan folk dance
Brainstorm on the social and economic roles of Kenyan folk dances in the community
Use available materials to make ornaments for use in performing a Kenyan folk dance using one-way technique (beadwork)
Explore making ornaments considering; colour variation, size of beads
Identify and take a role to perform a Kenyan folk dance adhering to performance components
coreCompetencies: Communication and collaboration — the learner uses dance performance as an avenue to communicate ideas, feelings and emotions
Creativity and Imagination — the learner uses various dance formations and patterns in a folk dance
Citizenship — the learner performs folk dances from diverse Kenya communities
linkedLearningAreas: Indigenous languages — the learner performs dance songs in indigenous languages
scopeNotes: include: background details are name, community of origin, performers (soloist, chorus/response, instrumentalist, dancers), and occasion
include: components are songs, costumes, body movements, adornment, ornaments, formations, props and instruments
include: performance components add formations AND patterns, and safety and etiquette
include: the social AND economic roles of folk dance in the community must both be discussed
include: the ornament is made with the one-way beading technique, considering colour variation and bead size
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric rewards performing/displaying a folk dance from a Kenyan indigenous community (Strand 2 rubric) and, in Strand 3, discussing a Kenyan folk dance elaborately.
subStrands.buildNotes: 5 QuestionKinds (multiple-choice, categorize, click-match, ordering, fill-blank). Dances named are real documented Kenyan folk dances across different communities: isukuti (Luhya), kilumi (Kamba), mwomboko (Kikuyu), chakacha (coastal), adumu (Maasai). No folk-dance/beadwork VisualSpec exists — omitted deliberately.

subStrands.name: 2.4 Puppetry
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify a glove puppet for familiarisation
Make a glove puppet using recyclable materials
Perform a puppet show while singing topical songs for enjoyment
keyInquiryQuestions: Why are features of a puppet exaggerated?
learningExperiences: Observe sample puppets in actual/virtual sources to identify a glove puppet for familiarisation
Explore the environment responsibly to gather recyclable materials for making glove puppets (found objects)
Make a glove puppet using recyclable materials with emphasis on functionality and exaggeration
Decorate the puppet to bring out features for aesthetics
Present a puppet show incorporating topical songs with proper voice projection and clarity in pronunciation of words (diction)
coreCompetencies: Creativity and imagination — the learner explores new materials and ideas when making puppets from recyclable materials
linkedLearningAreas: Science and Technology — the learner conserves the environment by recycling and upcycling found objects when making puppets
scopeNotes: include: puppet type is specifically the glove puppet
include: making it emphasises functionality (it fits the hand and moves) and exaggeration (features large enough to read at a distance)
include: decoration is for aesthetics; the show uses topical songs (about current issues), with voice projection and diction
note: this is a thin 8-lesson sub-strand — the build still reaches 5 QuestionKinds by branching identify / term-match / material-sort / make-order / show-true-false / reasoning / fill-blank
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric rewards performing/displaying a glove puppet.
subStrands.buildNotes: 5 QuestionKinds (multiple-choice, categorize, click-match, ordering, fill-blank). No puppet VisualSpec exists — omitted deliberately.

subStrands.name: 2.5 Descant Recorder
subStrandBullets: Notes B A G C1 D1
Playing Techniques: fingering, breath control, tonguing, tone quality
specificLearningOutcomes: Play notes B A G C1 D1 on the descant recorder
Play a melody built on the notes G A B C' D' on the descant recorder applying appropriate techniques
Create a random repeat pattern based on the notes B A G C1 D1 using a stencil
Enjoy playing melodies using the descant recorder
keyInquiryQuestions: How is a good tone produced on the descant recorder?
learningExperiences: Observe the baroque fingering chart for note C1 and D1 and practise fingering the notes
Responsibly search and watch a video/observe a demonstration on how to play notes C1 and D1
Play notes B A G C1 D1 on the descant recorder with appropriate techniques
Play simple melodies based on the notes B A G C1 D1 on the descant recorder applying appropriate playing techniques
Collaboratively create stencils of the notes B A G C1 D1
Print random repeat patterns on paper with the stencils using contrasting colours (dabbing/spraying method) and mount the patterns for display
Play melodies based on the notes B A G C1 D1 before peers for review
coreCompetencies: Digital literacy — the learner connects to digital resources to search for information on how notes are played on the descant recorder
Communication and Collaboration — the learner collaboratively with peers performs and creates stencils of the notes B A G C1 D1
linkedLearningAreas: English — the learner uses English as the language of communication in providing feedback on peers' performances of melodies on the descant recorder
scopeNotes: include: notes are exactly B A G C1 D1 (high C and high D), read from the baroque fingering chart
include: playing techniques are exactly fingering, breath control, tonguing, tone quality; 'how a good tone is produced' is the key inquiry
include: the craft output is a random repeat pattern of the note shapes, printed by stencil in contrasting colours (dabbing/spraying) and mounted
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric rewards performing/displaying a melody built on notes B A G C1 D1 on a descant recorder AND a random repeat pattern based on B A G C1 D1.
subStrands.buildNotes: 6 QuestionKinds (multiple-choice, categorize, click-match, ordering, number-line, fill-blank). Uses the registered { type: 'recorder-fingering' } VisualSpec for B A G C1 D1. number-line branch marks a note's pitch-order rank (G=1 .. D1=5).

subStrands.name: 2.6 Swimming (Optional — MUST choose ONE of Swimming OR Indigenous Kenyan Games)
specificLearningOutcomes: Describe the Front crawl technique in swimming
Perform the Front crawl technique for skill acquisition
Apply the front crawl technique in swimming for enjoyment
Appreciate own and others' efforts in performing the Front crawl technique
keyInquiryQuestions: Why is hygiene and safety necessary in swimming?
learningExperiences: Watch an actual or live performance of a Front crawl in swimming to talk about the skill
Demonstrate the front crawl skill in swimming (glide, body position, arm action, leg action and breathing) while inside the water
Practise Front crawl skill while ensuring smooth progression (leg, arm action, rhythm and tempo)
Swim using Front crawl in mini games while observing pool hygiene and safety
Talk about own and others' performance for feedback
coreCompetencies: Digital literacy — the learner uses digital devices to watch video clips of Front crawl in swimming
Learning to learn — the learner demonstrates and practises the Front crawl skills with persistence
linkedLearningAreas: Science and technology — the learner is exposed to the concept of floating
scopeNotes: include: the stroke is exactly the front crawl, broken into glide, body position, arm action, leg action and breathing
include: smooth progression means building up leg, then arm action, then rhythm and tempo
include: pool hygiene and safety, and why they matter, is the key inquiry
note: OPTIONAL sub-strand — the learner covers this OR 2.6 Indigenous Kenyan Games; this build ships both as separate skills
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric rewards performing/displaying Front crawl (or indigenous counting games).
subStrands.buildNotes: 5 QuestionKinds (multiple-choice, categorize, click-match, ordering, fill-blank). No swimming-stroke VisualSpec exists — omitted deliberately.

subStrands.name: 2.6 Indigenous Kenyan Games (Optional — MUST choose ONE of Swimming OR Indigenous Kenyan Games)
specificLearningOutcomes: Identify types of indigenous counting games played in Kenya
Perform different indigenous counting games for skill acquisition
Perform indigenous counting games to a musical rhythm
Appreciate the role played by counting games for fitness and health
keyInquiryQuestions: How do indigenous counting games enhance physical fitness?
learningExperiences: Watch a virtual or live demonstration of indigenous counting game and identify the skills
Demonstrate different indigenous counting games while observing safety
Collaboratively, practise different indigenous counting games while observing safety
Practise different types of indigenous counting games while combining it with musical rhythm
coreCompetencies: Communication and Collaboration — the learner works with others to practice indigenous counting games
Learning to learn — the learner acquires skills in indigenous counting games
linkedLearningAreas: Mathematics — the learner uses the knowledge of counting during the performance of the indigenous counting games
scopeNotes: include: the games are counting games — active playground games where players count aloud while doing a physical action
include: the games are performed to a musical rhythm
include: how counting games build physical fitness and health is the key inquiry
note: OPTIONAL sub-strand (alternative to 2.6 Swimming). Appendix II resources: counter, ropes, bean bags, counting video games
subStrands.assessmentSignal: Rubric rewards performing/displaying Front crawl/indigenous counting games.
subStrands.buildNotes: 5 QuestionKinds (multiple-choice, categorize, click-match, ordering, fill-blank). Games modelled: skipping-rope counting game, hopscotch, bean-bag toss-and-count, ball-catch counting game (kati-style), clapping-and-counting circle game. No counting-game VisualSpec exists — omitted deliberately.

subStrands.name: 3.1 Analysis of Creative Arts works
subStrandBullets: Components of a folk dance; community, occasion, participants, songs, body movement, formations, instruments, costumes, body adornment, ornament
East African Community Anthem: message, values, occasion and etiquette in performance
specificLearningOutcomes: Showcase artworks in a school gallery for critique
Discuss a Kenyan folk dance using appropriate terminologies
Discuss the East African Community Anthem to foster patriotism
Participate in ball games and athletics
Value appreciation of Creative Arts works drawn from various cultural backgrounds
keyInquiryQuestions: Why is it important to showcase Creative Arts works?
learningExperiences: Prepare display areas within the school with peers using available resources
Display artworks kept in the portfolio on the display areas within the school (drawings, painting, card, a puppet, decorated fabric, mosaic and ornaments)
Take a gallery walk and talk about own and others work considering; type of art, materials, media and aesthetic
Listen to selected folk dances from Kenyan communities and critically analyse the components

Listen to a recording/watch a performance of the East African Community Anthem (in unison) with peers and talk about it focussing on; its message, values, occasions when performed and etiquette in performance

scopeNotes: include: the gallery walk critiques each work by type of art, materials, media and aesthetic
